output.answer: RLHF assistants trade helpfulness against harmlessness: harmlessness training tends to make them evasive and quick to refuse, while helpfulness training makes them comply with harmful requests. Researchers have tried to reduce the tension by splitting good behavior into explicit rules with targeted human judgements (Sparrow) and by replacing human harmlessness labels with AI feedback guided by a written constitution, which yields a harmless but non-evasive assistant. Red teaming finds RLHF models get harder to attack as they scale.

output.answer: Safety training fails because helpfulness and safety objectives compete, and because safety behavior doesn't generalize to every domain where the model is capable. Refusal is also mechanistically shallow: one activation direction mediates it, and adversarial suffixes suppress that direction. Automated attacks exploit this by optimizing suffixes with gradients (GCG) or with random search on log-probabilities to force an affirmative start such as "Sure", reaching near-100% success on aligned models.

claims.text: Two failure modes of safety training are competing objectives and mismatched generalization.
claims.quote: We hypothesize two failure modes of safety training: competing objectives and mismatched generalization.

claims.text: Competing objectives arise when capability and safety goals conflict; mismatched generalization arises when safety training misses a domain the model can handle.
claims.quote: Competing objectives arise when a model's capabilities and safety goals conflict, while mismatched generalization occurs when safety training fails to generalize to a domain for which capabilities exist.

output.answer: Attackers plant instructions or false content in data the application will retrieve, such as web pages, documents, or a RAG knowledge base, so the model reads it as context and acts on it (indirect prompt injection) without the attacker ever talking to the model. Poisoning a RAG database with a few crafted passages can steer answers to attacker-chosen targets. Adaptive attacks bypass published defenses against indirect injection, which motivates system designs that keep untrusted data from controlling program flow.

output.answer: They keep the learning signal in text instead of weights. Reflexion agents write verbal reflections on task feedback into an episodic memory and reread them on the next trial. ExpeL gathers experiences across training tasks, extracts natural-language insights, and recalls insights and past trajectories at inference. Self-Refine has one model critique and revise its own output, and Voyager stores working code in a growing skill library and improves programs from environment feedback, all through black-box queries.

output.answer: Large LMs store much factual knowledge in their parameters and can rival retrieval systems on common questions, but they struggle with less popular, long-tail facts, and scaling helps little there. Retrieval-augmented models beat far larger parametric-only models on such facts, while unassisted models stay competitive on popular entities, so retrieving only when needed works well. Retrieval-augmented models such as RAG and Atlas also give more factual outputs and strong few-shot results with far fewer parameters.
